migrationNotes: Spine: a lone ferry owner on an island. We follow her decision from what one more passenger adds to her takings, to the line for marginal revenue, to the point where she stops selling and the price that follows, and then to the passengers she turns away compared with a crowd of rival boats.
Unused questions: econ-monopoly-mr-check (the line for P = 60 − Q; the marginal revenue line is now taught and tested by econ-monopoly-1). Its citation is removed.

Teaching examples (ferry with P = 50 − Q, MC £14) differ from every practice and worked item so no teaching screen gives away an answer. The marginal revenue line gives the discrete step of £29 as the midpoint of £30 and £28.
Prompts of econ-monopoly-3, -4 and -check-3 rewritten to stand alone; keys unchanged.

lesson.title: One seller

lead.text: A firm that is the only seller of what it sells is called a monopolist. The ferry owner is one: nobody else sells the crossing, so she does not take a price from a market. She sets it, and a firm that sets its own price is a price-maker. That does not leave her free to charge anything. At £60 hardly anyone would cross and at £5 almost everyone would, so the number of tickets she sells depends on the price she names.

That link is the demand curve from the earlier lessons, now seen from the seller's side. Say the island's demand is P = 50 − Q, where Q is the number of tickets sold in a day. Priced at £40, the boat carries 10 passengers; priced at £39, it carries 11. Carrying a passenger costs her £14 in fuel and wear on the boat, the same for everyone.
To pick a price she needs to know what an extra passenger is worth to her. The obvious answer is the ticket price, and it turns out to be wrong. The next screen shows why.

Suppose she charges £40, so 10 passengers cross and she takes in 10 × £40 = £400. To fill an eleventh seat she must drop the price to £39. The boat has one price for everyone, so all 11 pay £39 and her takings become 11 × £39 = £429. The extra passenger raised her takings by £29, which is well below the £39 ticket.

The shortfall has a simple cause. The new passenger pays £39, but the ten who were already travelling now pay £1 less each, and that costs her £10. So the extra revenue is £39 − £10 = £29. The extra revenue from selling one more unit is called marginal revenue. For the price-taking firms of the last lesson it equalled the price, because selling more never moved the price. A monopolist's price falls whenever she sells more, so her marginal revenue is always below the price.
The more passengers already travelling, the more each price cut costs, and the further marginal revenue drops below the price.
Use the same split as on the ferry: what the new unit sells for, less what the price cut costs on the units already selling.

Working this out one price at a time is slow, and for a straight demand curve there is a shortcut. With demand P = 50 − Q, the next ticket after Q sales pays about 50 − Q. Each extra ticket lowers the price by £1, and that £1 comes off all Q tickets already sold, which costs about £Q. That leaves 50 − Q − Q = 50 − 2Q.

In general, for demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is MR = a − 2bQ. It starts at the same price as demand and falls twice as fast. The figure draws both lines for the ferry, with a flat line for the £14 cost of carrying a passenger.

afterFigure.text: At 10 passengers the line gives £30, and the step from 10 to 11 was £29, which sits between the line's £30 at 10 and £28 at 11. The line reaches zero at 25 passengers, while demand does not reach zero until 50. The gold dot marks where the owner should stop selling, and the next screens show how to find it.

lead.text: A different seller faces demand P = 100 − Q. Use the marginal revenue line to find what its next unit is worth, and compare that with the price.

reveal.text: Marginal revenue is £40 while the price is £70. Each extra unit is worth much less to the seller than the price on the tag.

lead.text: Marginal revenue gives the owner something to weigh against her £14 cost. The rule is the one from the last lesson: a passenger is worth carrying while the sale adds more to her takings than to her costs. The sale adds marginal revenue, not the ticket price, so that is what she compares with £14.

With MR = 50 − 2Q the comparison is quick. With 10 passengers MR is £30, so another sale pays. Once there are 15 it is £20, which still pays. Reaching 18 it equals the £14 cost, and by 20 it has fallen to £10, so a sale there loses money. She stops where marginal revenue meets marginal cost: 50 − 2Q = 14, which gives Q = 18.

The price comes from demand. The 18 passengers will each pay 50 − 18 = £32, so that is the ticket price. She takes in 18 × £32 = £576, spends 18 × £14 = £252 and keeps £324. Comparing the price with the cost would have misled her. At 20 passengers the price is £30, far above £14, yet the twentieth sale adds only about £10.

lead.text: A new demand curve and cost. Write the marginal revenue line first, then set it equal to marginal cost.

reveal.text: You doubled the demand slope to get marginal revenue, then solved. At 12 units the monopolist charges £36.

lead.text: Now suppose the crossing were shared among many small boats, all competing for passengers. As the last lesson showed, sellers in competition end up charging the cost of one more unit, here £14. Demand P = 50 − Q gives 50 − Q = 14, so 36 passengers cross. The monopolist carries only 18 and charges £32.
So she sells half as many tickets at more than twice the competitive price. The figure shades the passengers in between.

afterFigure.text: Between 18 and 36 passengers, every crossing is worth more to the passenger than the £14 it costs to carry them. The nineteenth would pay up to £31 for a trip that costs £14. These trades never happen, because carrying the extra passenger means cutting the price for everyone and that costs her more than the passenger adds.

The lost value forms a triangle with base 36 − 18 = 18 and height £32 − £14 = £18, so its area is ½ × 18 × 18 = £162. It is the deadweight loss of monopoly, the same idea as the loss from a tax. Her £324 profit is value moved from passengers to her, but the £162 goes to nobody.

lead.text: The monopolist in the faded example faced P = 100 − Q with a marginal cost of £20 and sold 40 units. Find what competition would sell in the same market.
Now compare that monopoly with competition. Count the units that competition would sell and the monopoly does not.

reveal.text: The lost value is a triangle with base 40 and height £40: £800. The monopoly's profit is a transfer from buyers to the firm; the £800 is lost to everyone.

lesson.orientation: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output. Then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Every firm in the last lesson took its price from the market. A workshop could make as many units as it liked and each one sold at the going price, because it was one maker among many. Its only decision was how much to make.

Now take an island with a single ferry to the mainland, run by one family. Nobody else sells the crossing, so nobody can undercut her. The owner names a price and the islanders decide how many tickets to buy at it. A higher price keeps some people at home. A lower price fills the boat but brings in less from each passenger.

She has two things to settle, how much to charge and how many crossings to sell, and the two are linked. This lesson follows her decision. It starts with what an extra passenger really adds to her takings. From there it finds where she stops selling, and then it measures what that choice costs the island compared with ferries in competition.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a single seller's price and output from marginal revenue, and measure the value its pricing wastes.

recap.keyIdea: A monopolist's marginal revenue falls below its price, so it stops where MR meets MC and charges what demand allows. That is less output at a higher price than competition, and the units in between are a deadweight loss.

blocks.text: You found marginal revenue of £40 against a £70 price, and the ferry owner stopped at 18 passengers where competition would carry 36. In the £100 market the monopoly sold 40 units where competition sold 80, and £800 of value was lost.

recap.nextHook: The ferry owner had no rivals to watch. Next we look at a few firms that share a market, where each one's best choice depends on what the others do.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − Q, so marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 2Q. What is marginal revenue at Q = 30, in pounds?
hints: Substitute the quantity into the MR equation.
Double the quantity first.
Subtract that from the intercept.
questions.onCorrect: £40, well below the £70 price. A sole seller's extra unit is worth less than its price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price at 30 units. Marginal revenue is lower.
That is the intercept. Substitute the quantity into the equation.

questions.prompt: Price from the demand curve, in pounds
hints: Find the output where MR equals MC first.
Solve 100 − 2Q = MC.
Read the price from the demand curve at that output.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40, and the demand curve gives P = 100 − 40 = £60.

questions.onCorrect: £60. Output from MR = MC, then the price demand allows at that output.

misconceptions.feedback: That is marginal cost. Read the price from the demand curve.
That is the output. Put it into the demand curve.

questions.prompt: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is a constant £20. If the market were competitive, price would equal marginal cost. What quantity would be sold?
hints: Set the demand price equal to marginal cost.
Solve 100 − Q = MC.
Compare the result with the monopoly output.
questions.onCorrect: 80 units. Competition pushes price down to marginal cost, so the monopoly output is only half this.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the monopoly output. Competition sets price equal to marginal cost.
That is the price. The question asks for the quantity.

questions.prompt: In that market a monopoly sells 40 units at £60, while competition would sell 80 units at £20. What is the monopoly's deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: The lost units lie between the two quantities.
On them, the gap between buyers' value and marginal cost shrinks from the markup to zero.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £800. The 40 units never sold were each worth more to buyers than they cost to make.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 60 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £12. What is its profit-maximising quantity?
hints: With P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ.
Write the MR equation for this demand curve.
Set MR equal to marginal cost and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: MR = 60 − 4Q. Setting 60 − 4Q = 12 gives Q = 12, sold at P = 60 − 24 = £36.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units. Double the demand slope to get MR, then set it equal to marginal cost.

misconceptions.feedback: You used the demand slope for marginal revenue. MR falls twice as fast.
That is the price, not the quantity.

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market with the same costs, a profit-maximising monopoly…
hints: Marginal revenue lies below the demand curve.

acceptedIdeas: sells less at a higher price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost, and charges what demand allows for that smaller output.

choices.label: sells less at a higher price
sells more at a lower price
sells the same quantity at a higher price

questions.onCorrect: It sells less at a higher price: it stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost.

misconceptions.feedback: A monopoly restricts output; it does not expand it.
It cuts output where MR meets MC, short of the competitive quantity.

questions.prompt: A firm is the only seller of a product. It sells 30 units at £70 each. To sell 31 it must cut the price of every unit to £69. How much extra revenue does the 31st unit bring, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue at 31 units: 31 × 69 = £2,139. Revenue at 30: 30 × 70 = £2,100. The difference is £39.

hints: Revenue is price times units. Work it out at 30 units and at 31.
At 31 units every unit sells for the lower price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.
questions.onCorrect: £39. The new unit sells for £69, but the price cut costs £30 on the units already selling.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price of the new unit. The price cut also costs the units already selling.
That is what the price cut costs on the units already selling. The new unit adds revenue too.
That is the total revenue at 31 units. Subtract the revenue before.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces demand P = 60 − Q. Which is its marginal revenue line?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Marginal revenue starts at the same intercept as demand and falls twice as fast.

hints: Think about what a price cut costs on every unit already sold.
questions.onCorrect: MR = 60 − 2Q. Same intercept as demand, falling twice as fast, because each price cut applies to every unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the demand curve itself. Marginal revenue falls faster, because of the cut on units already selling.
The intercept stays the same as demand's. Only the slope doubles.

questions.prompt: Why not set price equal to marginal cost?

choices.label: The extra revenue from one more unit is MR, not the price: the price cut hits every unit.
Price is always equal to marginal cost for a monopolist.

acceptedIdeas: The extra revenue from one more unit is MR, not the price: the price cut hits every unit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selling one more means cutting the price on every unit, so the unit adds less than its price. The comparison with cost has to use MR.

hints: What does one more unit really add to revenue?
questions.onCorrect: Compare cost with what a unit adds to revenue, which is MR. The price overstates it.

misconceptions.feedback: Price is above marginal cost for a monopolist. That gap is the point.
Steepness changes the numbers, not the rule. The reason is what an extra unit adds to revenue.

hints: Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
Move the constant to one side.
Divide by the slope.
questions.onCorrect: 40 units. The monopolist stops where MR meets MC.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the competitive output, where price meets marginal cost.
That is the price, not the output.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 90 − Q and has a constant marginal cost of £30 and no fixed cost. What is its maximum profit, in pounds?
hints: Find the output where MR equals MC.
Read the price from demand at that output.
Profit is the price minus marginal cost, times the output.
questions.onCorrect: £900. Output from MR = MC, price from demand, then profit per unit times output.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue. Take off the cost.
That is the output. Find the profit on all those units.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 100 − 2Q with a constant marginal cost of £20. What is the deadweight loss of its pricing compared with competition, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Monopoly: MR = 100 − 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20, P = £60. Competition: 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40. Loss = ½ × (40 − 20) × (60 − 20) = £400.

hints: Find the monopoly output where MR equals MC, then the competitive output where price equals MC.
The lost units lie between those two quantities.
Take half of that base times the gap between the monopoly price and marginal cost.
questions.onCorrect: £400. A triangle between the two outputs, as tall as the monopoly's markup.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the monopoly output. Find the area of the lost triangle.
